1.pericope_label: The words of Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah, of the priests that were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin: To whom the word of the Lord came in the days of Josiah the son of Amon king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign. It came also in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, unto the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah the son of Josiah king of Judah, unto the carrying away of Jerusalem captive in the fifth month.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch open with the political weather, Assyria crushed since the destruction before the gates of Jerusalem, the Medes independent and Babylon in insurrection, so that Judah enjoyed unbroken peace at the call; Ellicott dates the king at twenty or twenty-one, presses the near coincidence of the prophet's beginning with the reformation, assumes the prophet was about twenty, and notes which short reigns the superscription passes over.

Gill takes the opening as the general title of the whole book and insists the words are the Lord's and not the prophet's own; Calvin sets the call against a religion wholly vitiated by the loss of the Book of the Law, calls the boy-conjecture frivolous, and doubts on chronological grounds whether the reforming king was his father's son by nature.

Clarke puts the prophet at probably fourteen, gives upwards of forty years of ministry ending in Egypt, and sketches the man who might have made terms with the enemy and chose the disasters instead; Wesley counts forty-one years in Judea besides Egypt and places Anathoth three miles from Jerusalem, allotted to the priests out of Benjamin.

Henry works the genealogy and the seasonableness together: not the high priest's son, a priest already authorized to teach with the prophet's commission added, raised up in the year after the young king began to purge the land.

debates.question: How old was the prophet when he was called?

positions.position: Probably fourteen.
Not a child: the word means a youth or a young man, and the conjecture that he was a boy is frivolous.
About twenty, which would make him sixty or sixty-one at the captivity.

debates.question: What were the times like when the call came?

positions.position: Unbroken peace, the Assyrian power long since crushed and its subject nations in revolt.
Extreme corruption, religion wholly vitiated because the Book of the Law had been lost.
A reformation newly begun, a young prophet raised up to assist and encourage a young king.

debates.question: Why are two reigns missing from the dating?

positions.position: Their brevity, and perhaps no word of the Lord came in that time.
Two reigns of three months each are passed over for the more conspicuous reigns of eleven years apiece.

outliers.claim: Reads the priesthood into the call: the man was already authorized to teach as a priest, and the extraordinary commission was added to that, God supporting an order then sadly eclipsed.

Doubts on chronological grounds whether the reforming king was his father's son by nature, since the father must have begotten him at fifteen, and suggests a son by law, as a later king is called son though many think him a nephew.

themes: The words of Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah, of the priests that were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin:
To whom the word of the Lord came in the days of Josiah the son of Amon king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign.

It came also in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, unto the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah the son of Josiah king of Judah, unto the carrying away of Jerusalem captive in the fifth month.

4.pericope_label: Then the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations. Then said I, Ah, Lord God! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child. But the Lord said unto me, Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak. Be not afraid of their faces: for I am with thee to deliver thee, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the excuse sharply from the one Moses made, since Moses lacked the gift of utterance while this man only thought himself unequal through youth, and hold that he was to publish no thoughts of his own but the counsel revealed to him; Ellicott reasons from the absence of dream or vision to a distinct consciousness of the voice within, makes the mission to the outlying nations the distinguishing characteristic of the work, and reads the same clause as saying exactly what Moses said.

Gill takes the being known before birth as knowledge with special love joined to it rather than bare omniscience, and reads the exclamation, with the Jewish commentators, as a word of distress and grief; Calvin gives two reasons for the recorded refusal, to clear the man of any suspicion of rashness and to make his hearers attentive, and traces the fear to a degenerate people long exulting in their freedom.

Clarke has the prophet first feel the inspiring influence of the Spirit, which gave the subjects and the words alike, and turns the shrinking into a test of ministry against those who run for worldly honour; Wesley reads sanctified as ordained to a public service, said to this prophet because he needed more encouragement, and hears in the answer a promise of eloquence and courage.

Henry hears the commission as to or against the nations, and puts the Jews first among them because they had learned the works of the nations and would not otherwise be numbered with them; and he keeps the office open, the prophet still telling nations what judgments follow national sins.

debates.question: What does the excuse that he cannot speak mean?

positions.position: Not what Moses said: Moses lacked the gift of utterance, while this man only thinks himself unequal through youth and inexperience.
Exactly what Moses said: not a man of words, having no gifts of utterance.

debates.question: Why is the refusal recorded at all?

positions.position: To clear the man of any suspicion of rashness, since many wish to be teachers, and to gain him esteem and attention.
As a mark of true calling: those really called know their own weakness, while those never called run for worldly honour.

debates.question: How wide is the commission to the nations?

positions.position: To the outlying Gentile nations, and this is the distinguishing characteristic of the work as against the other prophets.
To or against the nations, the Jews first among them because they had learned the works of the nations.

outliers.claim: Reasons from the silence about dream or vision to a distinct consciousness that the voice heard in the inmost soul was from Jehovah, revelation elsewhere presupposing a trance, a dream, or a training inward or outward.

Finds the cause of the fear in the hearers rather than the speaker: a degenerate people who had shaken off the yoke for years and were exulting in their freedom, so that the prophet refused indirectly and never confessed plainly how it stood.

themes: Then the word of the Lord came unto me, saying,
Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.
Then said I, Ah, Lord God! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child.
But the Lord said unto me, Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak.
Be not afraid of their faces: for I am with thee to deliver thee, saith the Lord.

9.pericope_label: Then the Lord put forth his hand, and touched my mouth. And the Lord said unto me, Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth. See, I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch argue from the organ, the hand being the instrument of making and doing, so that touching the mouth is an emblem of God framing there what the man is to speak, a tangible pledge of inspiration; Ellicott takes the act for something like a waking vision, identifies the hand of the Lord as the received symbol of the Spirit's influence, presses the word set to its literal sense of deputy, and reads the destroying and building as a sequence in time.

Gill reports the Jewish reading that an angel spoke in the Lord's name and prefers the Son of God in an assumed human form, and keeps the office to prophesying rather than ruling; Calvin makes the touched mouth a test of a true call, asks what prophets are sent for, and reads the investiture as showing how reverently God would have his word received when hardly one in a hundred receives it.

Clarke and Wesley both explain the idiom by which prophets are said to do what they foretell, Clarke setting beside it the command to make the heart of the people fat, while Wesley leaves the agent of the hand open and reads the rooting up and building as a condition offered to repentance.

positions.position: The Son of God, the true Jehovah, in a human form assumed for the occasion, against the Jewish reading that makes it an angel.
Either the hand of an angel or God himself in some visible shape.
Something like a waking vision, the hand of the Lord being the received symbol of the Spirit's special influence.

debates.question: Is the rooting up and building a condition or a sequence?

positions.position: A condition: repent and he will settle them in the land, refuse and he will pull them down.
A sequence in time: the work seems at first simply destructive, with the hope of construction beyond it, the whole sequel of the book a comment on the words.

debates.question: What does the touch of the mouth establish?

positions.position: An emblem that God frames in the mouth what the man is to speak, a tangible pledge of inspiration.
A test of a true call: the man brings nothing of his own but speaks as the oracles of God.
That the words are no more his own than those the apostles were to speak, which were put into their hearts by the Spirit of the Father.

outliers.claim: Reads the commission through an idiom, God representing his messengers as doing what he commanded them to declare, so that they rooted up by declaring judgments and built by declaring promises.

Turns the investiture on the hearers: there is no one who does not pretend to desire obedience, yet hardly one in a hundred really receives the word, some raising a clamour, others evading, others secretly opposing.

themes: Then the Lord put forth his hand, and touched my mouth. And the Lord said unto me, Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth.
See, I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant.

11.pericope_label: Moreover the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Jeremiah, what seest thou? And I said, I see a rod of an almond tree. Then said the Lord unto me, Thou hast well seen: for I will hasten my word to perform it.

schools.summary: Ellicott says the play on the tree's name cannot be reproduced, renders the answer literally as watching over the word to perform it, notes that the poetical and not the common name is used, and reads the bough as a token of hope, the early spring rising out of the dreariness of winter.

Gill puts the emblem in a line, a proper picture of what God is about to do and of the quick dispatch to be made in it; Calvin traces the derivation of the name, declines to render it almond at all, and objects that interpreters confine the promise too narrowly to the punishments that follow.

Clarke names the paronomasia and quotes the naturalist on the tree that blossoms in January and fruits in March, and takes the rod for the punishment about to be announced; Wesley coins an English verb for the pun and dates the miseries the portent foretold, from the death of the king to the captivity.

Henry reads the exchange as a lesson in method, God initiating the prophet in the prophetical learning and language, since prophets must have eyes as well as tongues and be seers as well as speakers; and he sees a correcting rod hanging over the people.

debates.question: What does the almond branch signify?

positions.position: A correcting rod hanging over the people, denoting affliction and chastisement.
The punishment about to be announced, a rod being an instrument of punishment.
A token of hope in contrast to the words of terror: the early spring rising out of the dreariness of winter, and a haste that will not delay a gracious promise.

debates.question: How is the play on words to be carried into English?

positions.position: By naming it a paronomasia and setting the two words side by side, the hastening tree against I will hasten.
It cannot be reproduced; render the sense literally, I too am watching over my word to perform it.
By coining a verb: I will almond-tree it, that is, I will be upon them speedily.
By declining to render the noun almond at all, since the verb behind it means to watch or hasten.

outliers.claim: Objects that interpreters unwisely confine the promise to the punishments mentioned afterwards; God is extolling his word as such, which does not vanish into air but is accompanied by power.

Reads the rod as a portent like a comet and dates the miseries it showed: the death of the king, the taxing under the king of Egypt, the breaking in of Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites, and at last the captivity.

themes: Moreover the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Jeremiah, what seest thou? And I said, I see a rod of an almond tree.
Then said the Lord unto me, Thou hast well seen: for I will hasten my word to perform it.

13.pericope_label: And the word of the Lord came unto me the second time, saying, What seest thou? And I said, I see a seething pot; and the face thereof is toward the north. Then the Lord said unto me, Out of the north an evil shall break forth upon all the inhabitants of the land. For, lo, I will call all the families of the kingdoms of the north, saith the Lord; and they shall come, and they shall set every one his throne at the entering of the gates of Jerusalem, and against all the walls thereof round about, and against all the cities of Judah. And I will utter my judgments against them touching all their wickedness, who have forsaken me, and have burned incense unto other gods, and worshipped the works of their own hands.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch deny that the verse about the thrones interprets the picture at all, calling it a direct statement of what was to fall on the inhabitants, and read the throne as the seat of sovereignty rather than of judgment; Ellicott corrects the rendering to from the north, describes the cauldron tipped to empty southward, lets the Scythians in beside the Chaldeans on a Greek historian's authority, and makes the calling a present, the evil already begun.

Gill keeps the northern families within one jurisdiction and reports that their calling is no more than putting it into their hearts to come, and settles the judgments as uttered against this people and not against the north; Calvin asks why the vision comes as question and answer, and rejects as strained the exposition that refers the judgments to the Chaldeans.

Clarke reports two constructions of the pot and refuses to decide between them, stops at the verb that means shall be opened, and notes that more than a hundred manuscripts read the singular work, idolatry being their one trade; Wesley makes the pot the besieging army and the face the front of the furnace, and takes the thrones for tents pitched.

positions.position: Either Judea agitated by the invasion, or the northern empire pouring out its multitudes; either suits the text.
A great cauldron on a pile of burning wood, tipped to empty its scalding contents southward.
The Babylonian army, besieging the city as a fire plays round a pot.

debates.question: What is meant by setting up thrones at the gates?

positions.position: The establishing of dominion, the throne being the seat of sovereignty and not of judgment.
The usurpation of justice, thrones of judgment set up where kings had sat to hear complaints.
Seats, pavilions or tents pitched, which shall be as so many thrones.

debates.question: Against whom are the judgments uttered, and what do they amount to?

positions.position: Against this people, not against the kingdoms of the north.
Against this people; the exposition that refers them to the Chaldeans is strained and confuted by what follows.
A lawsuit with someone, an expression peculiar to this prophet, comprehending trial and sentence and not merely remonstrance.

outliers.claim: Marks the cauldron as the strongest possible contrast to the vernal beauty of the almond-bough, and its boiling water as going beyond the waters of the great river in the older symbolism.

Asks why the vision is given as question and answer, and answers that a bare picture with an explanation appended would have had less force, while God set forth as present and explaining proves himself the author of the prophecy.

themes: And the word of the Lord came unto me the second time, saying, What seest thou? And I said, I see a seething pot; and the face thereof is toward the north.
Then the Lord said unto me, Out of the north an evil shall break forth upon all the inhabitants of the land.

For, lo, I will call all the families of the kingdoms of the north, saith the Lord; and they shall come, and they shall set every one his throne at the entering of the gates of Jerusalem, and against all the walls thereof round about, and against all the cities of Judah.
And I will utter my judgments against them touching all their wickedness, who have forsaken me, and have burned incense unto other gods, and worshipped the works of their own hands.

17.pericope_label: Thou therefore gird up thy loins, and arise, and speak unto them all that I command thee: be not dismayed at their faces, lest I confound thee before them. For, behold, I have made thee this day a defenced city, and an iron pillar, and brasen walls against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, against the princes thereof, against the priests thereof, and against the people of the land. And they shall fight against thee; but they shall not prevail against thee; for I am with thee, saith the Lord, to deliver thee.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the girding as fastening up the long garment to make a man fit for labour, a journey or a race, and render the warning with its repetition intact; Ellicott passes over the wardrobe for the messenger's readiness, reads a constitutional timidity out of the repeated calls to courage, and identifies the pillar that carries an eastern roof and the plates of copper fastened over a fortification.

Gill takes the loins of mind and body alike and notes that four versions read the promise as a comparison, a city that cannot be taken; Calvin puts the caution the images invite, that invincible power and great trials came together, and draws the rule that a promised victory is no occasion for torpor.

Clarke will not rest in the threat and offers two ways out of it, keeps the three images simple and observes that the issue proved the promise, and quotes an ancient line about being safe at sea upon a twig; Wesley keeps the sting of the warning and hears in the whole land that the troubles would be not only great but long.

debates.question: What does girding the loins picture?

positions.position: The eastern custom of trussing long garments so that the body is not impeded, for haste in the work.
The readiness of a messenger to be swift on his errand and go wherever he is sent.

debates.question: What does the clause lest I confound thee mean?

positions.position: Not a threat: God is often said to do what he only permits, or else the clause is reassurance, do not fear that I shall confound thee before them.
A threat kept intact, the Hebrew repeating the same word for emphasis: be not dismayed, lest I dismay thee.
A threat of destruction in their sight, to become their reproach.

debates.question: What do the three images promise?

positions.position: Immunity proved by the event: the prophet outlived every insult and saw his enemies carried away.
Strength heaped on strength: attacked as the cities were, but with a different issue, for they fall and he holds out.
Power to fight manfully, not exemption from danger or from anything grievous to the flesh.

outliers.claim: Reads a temperament out of the repeated calls to courage, a constitutional timidity like the one the letters to a young colleague address, excused by a recent reign in which the prophet's work could easily end in the martyr's fate.
Reports that four versions read the promise as a comparison, as a defenced city, one that cannot be taken.

themes: Thou therefore gird up thy loins, and arise, and speak unto them all that I command thee: be not dismayed at their faces, lest I confound thee before them.

For, behold, I have made thee this day a defenced city, and an iron pillar, and brasen walls against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, against the princes thereof, against the priests thereof, and against the people of the land.
And they shall fight against thee; but they shall not prevail against thee; for I am with thee, saith the Lord, to deliver thee.
